name: Steam cabinet

lead: A steam cabinet is a small enclosure, often with the head outside, that fills with steam so the body sweats in a compact space. It is a portable version of the steam bath tradition.
People use it for relaxation and for a warm, flushed skin look afterwards. Research on heat bathing is mostly about Finnish saunas, and no trials of steam cabinets for appearance were found.

paras: Users sit inside for a session, then cool down and rinse. Some pair it with skincare or recovery routines; session lengths and temperatures are set by manufacturer instructions.

Wet heat near 100% humidity can scald if too hot, and metal jewellery or glasses can burn. Sauna and steam guidance cautions people with heart conditions, low blood pressure or pregnancy, and warns against use with alcohol or drugs.

angle.text: Users report a warm, glowing skin look and relaxation after sessions, and some include it in recovery routines.

lead: A steam cabinet is an enclosed unit in which a person sits in steam, sometimes with the head outside, as a compact alternative to a steam room. The steam bath tradition includes Greek laconica, Roman thermae, the hammam and Mesoamerican temazcales.[1]

People use steam to promote sweating, relaxation and a warm, flushed skin look. Hammams were traditionally thought to soothe the body and remove toxins, though that claim is flagged as lacking citation in Wikipedia.[1]

Research on heat bathing is mostly on Finnish saunas, where long-term use is associated with lower sudden cardiac death risk, while evidence is described as insufficient for skin disorders.[2] No studies of steam cabinets for appearance were found.

paras: Steam baths run at lower temperatures than dry saunas, around 50 C, because wet heat can scald at higher settings.[2]

Metal jewellery and glasses can become hot enough to burn, and contact lenses can dry out.[2] Sauna guidance lists alcohol, dehydration and narcotics as raising sudden-death risk, and cautions for unstable angina, severe aortic stenosis and pregnancy.[2]
No studies found. Studies of Finnish saunas link frequent use to lower cardiovascular risk, with evidence for skin disorders described as insufficient.[2]
